instruction:
FIX-ROUND R1 for slice 020b2 (WP-SCP-020 §4 020B.2). R1 found 8 CRIT+MAJ. Close all of them; MIN/nit are recorded but don't block.

## Findings to close

### CORR-001 [MAJ, lens=correctness]
**Claim:** CI workflow hardcodes OPA and Conftest SHA256 values inline instead of reading them from scripts/scp-policy-check.lock, violating the single-source-of-truth requirement of AC (v).
**Evidence:** policy-check.yml:116 OPA_SHA256='50678b87...', :118 CONFTST_SHA256='e8144c6d...' (linux-x64); :122 OPA_SHA256='a6facfdd...', :124 CONFTST_SHA256='4005441...' (linux-arm64). The local script reads both digests at runtime via json_lock_field (scp-policy-check:136, :180-181). These values currently match the lockfile, but no machine-enforced binding exists. A lockfile-only bump (e.g. dependabot/Renovate PR touching scripts/.tool-versions and scp-policy-check.lock) leaves policy-check.yml verifying the stale digest until a separate manual edit is made.
**Impact:** After any version-bump commit that updates only the lockfile, CI will download the new binary and verify it against the old hardcoded SHA; verification will fail and CI will become non-functional. Alternatively, if the workflow SHA is updated but the lockfile is not, local repro accepts a different binary than CI. Either way the parity guarantee collapses on first bump.
**Mitigation:** Replace the hardcoded SHA block in the 'Install pinned OPA and Conftest runtimes' step with inline python3 that reads scripts/scp-policy-check.lock, keying on the detected arch (linux-x64 / linux-arm64). Use the same json_lock_field logic already implemented in the local script. This makes the lockfile the single authoritative source for both paths.

### CORR-002 [MAJ, lens=correctness]
**Claim:** CI verifies the Conftest tarball using the archive_sha256 field; the local script verifies the extracted binary using the sha256 field. These are different lockfile fields representing different digests; the fields are never cross-checked between the two paths.
**Evidence:** policy-check.yml:118,124: CONFTST_SHA256 equals lockfile.conftest.{linux-x64,linux-arm64}.archive_sha256 (archive-level digest). After tar extraction at policy-check.yml:175 there is no further verification. scp-policy-check:180 reads json_lock_field conftest $platform_key sha256 (binary-level digest) and verifies the extracted binary at :217. For linux-x64: archive_sha256='e8144c6d...' (CI), sha256='21d9651c...' (local) — two entirely different hex strings. CI never checks '21d9651c...'; local never checks 'e8144c6d...'.
**Impact:** The two verification paths are semantically disjoint. While archive SHA integrity implies binary integrity for an intact tarball, a future refactor that separates archive verification from extraction, or that uses a pre-extracted vendored binary, could produce a binary that passes one check but not the other. The inconsistency also makes auditing the supply-chain posture ambiguous: an auditor reading the CI step cannot determine whether the binary sha256 in the lockfile was ever checked by CI.
**Mitigation:** After CORR-001 lands and CI reads the lockfile: add an explicit binary SHA verification step after tar extraction, using the sha256 field from the lockfile. Mirror the local script's verify_file_sha call on ${BIN_DIR}/conftest. This aligns CI and local to an identical two-stage verification sequence.

### CORR-003 [MAJ, lens=correctness]
**Claim:** Changed-files discovery uses incompatible semantics between CI (two-SHA git diff of committed history) and local repro (staged/unstaged working-tree diff), making it impossible to reproduce the CI verdict locally for multi-commit PRs.
**Evidence:** CI 'Collect changed files' step at policy-check.yml:223: git diff --name-only "${SCP_BASE_SHA}..${SCP_HEAD_SHA}" -- "${SCP_FIXTURE_PATH}". Local prepare_changed_files at scp-policy-check:243-246: first tries git diff --name-only --cached (staged changes against HEAD), falls back to git diff --name-only (unstaged changes). For a PR with commits A→B→C, CI evaluates the full A..C diff. Local on a clean working tree at C evaluates an empty staged set, triggering the unstaged fallback which is also empty at C — net result: zero targets, scp_policy_check_run returns 0, false-pass. For a single-commit PR with a staged fix, local evaluates only that staged hunk, not earlier commits in the branch.
**Impact:** AC (v) requires identical inputs and identical invocation to CI. The changed-files list is the primary Conftest input. A developer running python -m standards_control_plane.policy_check locally receives a verdict that can silently diverge from CI's verdict. False-pass scenarios allow policy-violating commits to reach CI where they are caught instead of locally.
**Mitigation:** Add SCP_BASE_SHA and SCP_HEAD_SHA env-var awareness to prepare_changed_files. When both are set, replace the staged/unstaged heuristic with git diff --name-only "${SCP_BASE_SHA}..${SCP_HEAD_SHA}" -- "${SCP_FIXTURE_PATH:-.}" matching CI exactly. Preserve the existing staged/unstaged path as the default when SHAs are absent. Document the env vars in --help output and in the ADOPT-001 §12 pre-commit hook snippet.

### R1-SBP-MAJ-01 [MAJ, lens=safety]
**Claim:** The SCP_POLICY_CHECK_LOCKFILE, SCP_POLICY_CHECK_OPA_BASE_URL, and SCP_POLICY_CHECK_CONFTEST_BASE_URL environment variables can be combined by any caller to fully neutralise the SHA256 verification invariant. The verification model is: compute SHA256 of downloaded binary, compare against value in $LOCKFILE. If an adversary controls both the lockfile path and the download URL, they supply a crafted lockfile with attacker-chosen expected SHAs and serve matching binaries — the comparison passes. The Python wrapper (policy_check.py line 59: \`env = dict(os.environ)\`) forwards the entire calling environment to the shell script with no filtering, no documentation of the security-sensitive vars, and no warning when they override defaults. The test suite normalises this override pattern across all three test cases, making it invisible as a threat surface.
**Evidence:** scripts/scp-policy-check lines 6-8 define TOOL_VERSIONS_FILE, LOCKFILE, CACHE_ROOT via env overrides with no restriction. Lines 147, 193: base URL overrides accepted without constraint. src/standards_control_plane/policy_check.py lines 59-66: \`env = dict(os.environ)\` then \`subprocess.run([str(script_path), *args], env=env)\` — all env vars forwarded verbatim. tests/scripts/test_scp_policy_check.py lines 86-96: test sets SCP_POLICY_CHECK_LOCKFILE, SCP_POLICY_CHECK_OPA_BASE_URL, SCP_POLICY_CHECK_CONFTEST_BASE_URL simultaneously. No SECURITY.md note or inline warning on these vars.
**Impact:** An adversary who can inject environment variables into a pre-commit hook invocation, a CI step that calls scripts/scp-policy-check, or the Python entrypoint can execute an arbitrary binary with zero SHA256 resistance. The attack surface is any execution context where env is not locked down — common in shared CI systems, Docker-in-Docker setups, and developer workstations with profile-level env injection.
**Mitigation:** (1) Add a prominently commented SECURITY WARNING block in scripts/scp-policy-check near lines 6-8 listing SCP_POLICY_CHECK_LOCKFILE, SCP_POLICY_CHECK_OPA_BASE_URL, SCP_POLICY_CHECK_CONFTEST_BASE_URL as security-sensitive overrides that disable supply-chain guarantees. (2) In policy_check.py, strip or warn on these vars when they deviate from repo-default values (e.g. \`if 'SCP_POLICY_CHECK_LOCKFILE' in os.environ: warn to stderr\`). (3) Consider a --allow-env-override explicit flag rather than silent env acceptance for the base-URL overrides. (4) Document these vars under a 'Testing-only overrides' heading in ADOPT-001 §12.

### R1-SBP-MAJ-02 [MAJ, lens=safety]
**Claim:** lib/policy_check_invocation.sh contains no \`set -euo pipefail\` guard at the top level. When sourced in an environment where errexit and nounset are not active, function-level failures silently propagate as success. This is a latent hazard: the CI step at policy-check.yml line 238-240 sets \`set -euo pipefail\` inline before sourcing, and scripts/scp-policy-check sets it at line 2, so current invocation paths are protected. However the lib is designed for external sourcing and carries no self-protection. Any future script, pre-commit hook, or CI step that sources the lib without explicit errexit will silently swallow failures in conftest invocations, Python subprocess calls, and output-directory creation, potentially producing a false-pass verdict.
**Evidence:** lib/policy_check_invocation.sh: no \`set -euo pipefail\` anywhere in the file (grep confirmed no match). scripts/scp-policy-check line 2: \`set -euo pipefail\` present — protects sourcing of lib at line 287. policy-check.yml 'Run shared policy-check invocation' step lines 237-240: \`set -euo pipefail\` present — also protected. But lib itself cannot enforce this invariant if sourced standalone. lib/policy_check_invocation.sh lines 92-96: \`while IFS= read -r target; do ... done < "$changed_files_path"\` — if changed_files_path does not exist, this silently produces an empty targets array rather than erroring, because \`< file\` in a non-errexit shell returns non-zero but is suppressed.
**Impact:** An operator who writes a wrapper script or CI step and sources lib/policy_check_invocation.sh without \`set -euo pipefail\` will receive a passing exit code when conftest fails, the policy bundle is missing, or Python throws. The policy-check verdict is silent-pass on infra failure, violating the fail-closed contract in plan §4 020B (viii).
**Mitigation:** Add \`set -euo pipefail\` as the first non-comment line of lib/policy_check_invocation.sh. Since the lib is sourced (not executed), this only affects callers who source it — the typical pattern. Alternatively add a guard function \`scp_policy_check_assert_strict_mode() { ... }\` called at the top of scp_policy_check_run that verifies \`$-\` contains 'e' and 'u', emitting SCP-E001 and returning 1 if not.

### R1-SBP-MAJ-03 [MAJ, lens=safety]
**Claim:** TOCTOU race between SHA256 verification of a cached binary and its execution via PATH extension. ensure_cached_binary() (lines 112-123) checks file existence, verifies SHA256, then returns the verified path. The calling code adds the directory to PATH (line 275). No file descriptor or flock is held on the binary between verification and execution. A concurrent process with write access to the cache directory can replace the binary in this window.
**Evidence:** scripts/scp-policy-check lines 112-123: ensure_cached_binary reads path, calls verify_file_sha, then returns — no lock held. Line 275: \`export PATH="$(dirname "$OPA_BIN"):$(dirname "$CONFTST_BIN"):${PATH}"\` — extends PATH without re-reading the file. Line 162: \`install -m 0755 "$tmp_path" "$binary_path"\` — install is atomic on Linux (rename) but does not hold a lock across subsequent exec. No \`flock\`, \`lockfile\`, or \`/proc/self/fd\` pin anywhere in the script. The cache directory defaults to \`~/.cache/scp/\` (line 8) with world-readable mode (no chmod on mkdir output).
**Impact:** On single-user ephemeral CI runners (ubuntu-24.04) exploitability is negligible. On shared developer machines, Docker containers with shared-volume mounts, or remote dev boxes with multiple co-tenants, a process running as the same user can win the race and replace the verified binary with a malicious one before the conftest invocation at lib/policy_check_invocation.sh line 118. The gap is wider for conftest (larger binary, longer verification time) than OPA.
**Mitigation:** After install, open the binary file descriptor and exec via /proc/self/fd/N (Linux) or equivalent, eliminating the path-based race. Simpler: after PATH extension, hash the binary again immediately before the conftest/opa call in scp_policy_check_run (second verify at exec point). Alternatively restrict cache dir permissions: \`mkdir -p -m 0700 "$cache_dir"\` so only the owning user can write, limiting the race to same-uid scenarios where the attacker already has full user access.

### F-001 [MAJ, lens=completeness]
**Claim:** CI workflow hardcodes binary SHA256 values inline, independent of scripts/scp-policy-check.lock, creating a dual-source-of-truth for security-critical hash values that will diverge silently on any version bump.
**Evidence:** grep 'scp-policy-check\.lock' .github/workflows/policy-check.yml returns no matches. policy-check.yml:116-128 hardcodes OPA_SHA256 and CONFTST_SHA256 values (e.g., OPA x86_64 SHA256='50678b87...') in a case block. The identical values exist in scripts/scp-policy-check.lock under opa.linux-x64.sha256 and conftest.linux-x64.archive_sha256 respectively, but the workflow reads neither the lockfile nor any derived file from it for binary integrity. The 'Install pinned OPA and Conftest runtimes' step reads scripts/.tool-versions for version strings but uses only its own inline SHAs.
**Impact:** When a Renovate/Dependabot version-bump PR arrives and the operator updates scripts/.tool-versions and scripts/scp-policy-check.lock, the inline SHAs in policy-check.yml remain stale. The CI then (a) downloads the new binary version, (b) verifies it against the old SHA, and (c) fails with a spurious 'verification failed' error or, worse, silently succeeds if the new binary happens to share a hash prefix. No CI check enforces lockfile ↔ workflow SHA parity. This directly undermines the supply-chain security rationale for 020B(v).
**Mitigation:** In the 'Install pinned OPA and Conftest runtimes' step, replace hardcoded SHA256 case blocks with a python3 one-liner that reads scripts/scp-policy-check.lock at runtime: OPA_SHA256=$(python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(open('scripts/scp-policy-check.lock')); print(d['opa']['linux-${ARCH_KEY}']['sha256'])"). Alternatively, add a dedicated CI step (gateable on any PR that touches scripts/.tool-versions or scripts/scp-policy-check.lock) that asserts inline SHAs equal lockfile values. Either approach closes the dual-source gap before 020D1.

### F-002 [MAJ, lens=completeness]
**Claim:** The reusable workflow sources lib/policy_check_invocation.sh and reads scripts/.tool-versions from the checked-out caller workspace; external repos do not have these SCP-internal files, making the workflow non-functional for any downstream adopter outside SCP itself.
**Evidence:** policy-check.yml 'Checkout caller repository' step uses actions/checkout with no repository: override — it checks out the calling repo (${{ github.repository }}). Subsequent step at line 103 reads scripts/.tool-versions from that workspace via read_tool_version(). Step at line 239 executes 'source lib/policy_check_invocation.sh' — also relative to the caller workspace. No additional checkout step fetches the SCP repo to supply these files. For SCP self-use (020D1), the caller IS SCP, so both files are present. For any external caller (WP-SCP-024: pim, recommender, shopify-app, control-tower, etc.) neither file will exist.
**Impact:** FLA pilot (020I), CT pilot (WP-SCP-024 first target), and all downstream estate consumers will encounter either 'missing OPA version pin in scripts/.tool-versions' or 'lib/policy_check_invocation.sh: No such file or directory' at workflow boot. Adopters cannot work around this by adding a secrets: or env: override — the absence is structural. This is a blocking gap for the stated mission of 020 as an estate-wide primitive, even though it does not impair the current 020B.2 SCP-self scope.
**Mitigation:** Add an additional actions/checkout step early in the reusable workflow that fetches the SCP repo at the same SHA the workflow was dispatched from (using github.action_repository and github.action_ref or a hard-coded SHA comment-tag), placing it at path: .scp-runtime. Then replace 'source lib/policy_check_invocation.sh' with 'source .scp-runtime/lib/policy_check_invocation.sh' and 'scripts/.tool-versions' references with '.scp-runtime/scripts/.tool-versions'. SCP self-use continues to work unchanged (SCP's own files remain in the workspace root; the .scp-runtime path is the canonical runtime source). Address before 020D1 when the wrapper is written and any CI reference to the reusable workflow is published.
